name: Technical Credibility Through Non-Production Demonstrators
consequences: Delivering two working demonstrators (mobile-based FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS and a browser or hardware-token fallback path) proves that platform-neutral authentication is technically feasible without Apple or Google as trust anchors. This evidence shifts procurement and standards conversations from theoretical concern to concrete architectural option, though demonstrators do not integrate with live MitID and do not establish production-readiness or operator acceptance.
options: Develop a GrapheneOS-based FIDO2/WebAuthn authenticator coupled to a simulated OpenID Connect identity provider to show secure standards-based mobile authentication independent of platform app stores and integrity APIs.

Build a stateless hardware-token (FIDO2 with USB or NFC) paired with a simplified web-portal authentication flow that bypasses mobile OS entirely, demonstrating a resilience path for critical public access during platform disruption or policy conflict.

Create a browser-extension-based fallback authenticator using open cryptographic libraries and ephemeral trust anchors, showing that meaningful authentication can operate on commodity browsers without requiring app-store distribution or platform vendor consent.
review: Non-production demonstrators establish technical feasibility but do not address operator or regulatory reluctance to deploy platform-neutral paths in production, nor do they resolve the certification and audit burden required for formal Danish public-sector acceptance under eIDAS or NSIS frameworks.

name: Resilience Framing and Procurement Language
consequences: Reframing the issue away from privacy ideology toward supplier concentration, continuity-of-service risk, and strategic autonomy creates political traction with public-sector procurement offices and policy committees that respond to business continuity language rather than digital sovereignty rhetoric. This reframing also unlocks engagement with institutional stakeholders (risk management, compliance, audit) who would dismiss the issue if presented solely as a civil-liberties concern.
options: Commission an independent risk audit of MitID's platform dependency surface (app-store distribution, integrity API reliance, push-notification infrastructure) and present findings to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's continuity-planning and procurement divisions as a supplier-concentration exposure requiring mitigation language in future RFPs.

Draft formal policy proposals to relevant Danish government bodies and Folketinget committees that specify platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements in digital identity procurement, using language drawn from NIST cybersecurity frameworks and EU resilience directives rather than privacy advocacy.

Engage with Danish public-sector CISOs, chief information officers, and enterprise-architecture working groups to position platform-neutral authentication as a business-continuity and disaster-recovery requirement, building internal government demand for supplier diversification in identity infrastructure.
review: Procurement language and resilience framing can influence future RFP design, but existing operators (MitID, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen) have entrenched dependencies and institutional inertia that will interpret new requirements as costly retrofits rather than systemic improvements, especially if funding and timeline pressure favor the status quo.

name: Coalition Building Across Civil Society, Academia, and Standards Bodies
consequences: Establishing a coalition spanning privacy advocates, security researchers, contingency-planning stakeholders, and Folketinget members amplifies the project's credibility and distributes advocacy load across multiple institutions with independent standing. A multi-stakeholder coalition also creates policy pressure that a single research institution cannot generate alone, and it seeds longer-term institutional capacity for digital-sovereignty discourse in Denmark.
options: Convene a formal advisory board including representatives from civil-society organizations, academic security research centers, Danish industry association representatives, and sympathetic parliamentarians, meeting quarterly to review technical findings and coordinate input to government consultations.

Partner with European privacy and digital-rights organizations and EU standards bodies (ETSI, relevant eIDAS2 working groups) to position Danish platform-neutrality work as a test case for broader European requirements on interoperability and reduced platform lock-in, creating external validation and standards pressure.

Establish a public working group or research consortium that includes Aarhus University, University of Copenhagen, or equivalent security research centers, creating institutional capacity and peer review that lends authority to the project's findings and ensures continuity beyond the initial 24-month period.
review: Coalition-building increases advocacy reach but does not directly overcome institutional inertia within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or MitID operations, nor does it resolve the political difficulty of imposing new requirements on incumbent operators who will argue that compliance costs and deployment timelines are prohibitive.

name: AltID Procurement Timing and Standards Integration
consequences: Inserting platform-neutrality and fallback-access language into AltID's design requirements, procurement process, or formal standards materials before the system hardens creates the opportunity to influence architecture at the decision point where change is least costly. If procurement specifications do not include these requirements by month 18–20, retrofitting becomes prohibitively expensive and future systems risk replicating the same MitID dependencies.
options: Map AltID's procurement timeline, design-review gates, and standards-integration milestones, then time the project's policy proposals and demonstrator releases to align with decision points where specifications are still malleable, using early engagement with the AltID program management office to shape RFP language.

Submit formal comments and technical specifications to relevant EU-level eIDAS2 and European Digital Identity Wallet working groups, positioning Danish requirements as aligned with broader European resilience and interoperability goals, thereby creating top-down standards pressure that AltID procurement cannot easily ignore.

Negotiate a formal advisory role or review slot for the project team within AltID's governance structure or technical-working groups, allowing real-time input to architecture and procurement decisions rather than relying on post-hoc consultation or comment periods that typically occur too late to influence design.
review: Even well-timed procurement intervention may fail if AltID program leadership interprets platform-neutrality requirements as cost-additive or schedule-delaying, or if incumbent platform providers lobby successfully to frame the requirements as technically unnecessary, shifting risk to later remediation phases.

name: External Security Review and Institutional Legitimacy
consequences: Commissioning independent security audits and third-party reviews of the demonstrators and feasibility findings establishes credibility with skeptical stakeholders (operators, regulators, government IT planners) who would discount findings from a single advocacy-oriented research team. External review also identifies technical gaps and builds the institutional legitimacy needed to influence procurement and standards language.
options: Engage a recognized EU or international security certification body to conduct a formal technical review of the demonstrators and fallback-authentication architecture, producing a published assessment that establishes security sufficiency without requiring full production certification under eIDAS or NSIS.

Commission an independent policy and regulatory analysis from a respected Danish law and governance firm or university research center, assessing legal and compliance feasibility of platform-neutral requirements under Danish, EU, and eIDAS frameworks, and documenting blockers and solutions explicitly.

Arrange peer-review publication of the feasibility report in an academic or industry conference (e.g., IEEE security, ACM CCS, or EU digital-governance venues), creating scholarly validation and distancing the findings from advocacy-only messaging, while also ensuring findings remain accessible to non-academic stakeholders.
review: External review enhances credibility but cannot guarantee that regulatory bodies or operators will accept findings or act on recommendations, especially if institutional politics or vendor pressure favor maintaining the status quo despite acknowledged resilience risks.

name: Contingency Planning and Graceful De-Escalation
consequences: Planning explicitly for weak institutional engagement or procurement resistance ensures the project delivers measurable value even if formal AltID integration fails. Published feasibility reports, academic validation, and EU-standards input remain institutionally valuable and seed long-term digital-sovereignty capacity, even if immediate procurement traction is limited. De-escalation pathways also protect project credibility and team morale if political or vendor resistance proves stronger than anticipated.
options: Define phase-three success metrics that distinguish between strong-traction outcomes (formal procurement language, operator commitment) and weaker-traction outcomes (published reports, EU standards input, coalition consolidation), ensuring the project achieves measurable deliverables regardless of procurement responsiveness.

Establish a 'floor plan' for phase three that explicitly de-scopes away from direct AltID influence if phase-one engagement signals weak institutional receptivity, instead prioritizing publication, EU-level standards engagement, and coalition consolidation as alternative leverage points with longer time horizons.

Build contingency budget and timeline reserves into phase three to allow the project to pivot toward academic publication, industry-standards-body engagement, or EU eIDAS2 working-group participation if domestic procurement intervention does not materialize as planned, maintaining strategic value without overcommitting to unlikely institutional outcomes.
review: Contingency planning protects project delivery but risks appearing defeatist or undermining commitment to domestic procurement leverage if communicated prematurely, and it does not resolve the underlying institutional inertia or vendor resistance that may necessitate de-escalation in the first place.

name: Financing Stability and Gated-Phase Release Strategy
consequences: Distributing funding across three phases with conditional gates (phase two funded only if phase one produces a published report and documented institutional engagement; phase three funded only if phase two demonstrates technical feasibility) ensures that funds are released only when concrete progress validates further investment. This gating protects against sunk costs and creates institutional accountability, but it also introduces schedule risk if gate conditions are not met on time.
options: Secure all 10.5 million DKK in conditional commitments from Danish public sources (e.g., research councils, government digital-strategy budgets, or EU Horizon-Europe co-funding) before project start, with explicit gate conditions tied to phase-one deliverables and documented institutional engagement, reducing financing uncertainty and demonstrating donor confidence.

Implement a rolling funding model where phase-one funding (3.0 million DKK) is released immediately, but phase-two and phase-three funding are secured through additional grant rounds or institutional partnerships tied to demonstrator delivery and procurement-engagement milestones, creating flexibility for scope adjustment based on phase-one findings.

Establish a hybrid financing model combining research council grants (phases one and two) with EU co-funding or venture-style impact investment for phase three, diversifying financing risk and creating incentives for EU-level standards engagement while maintaining gated release to Danish procure ment milestones.
review: Gated funding protects project accountability but introduces scheduling risk if phase-one deliverables slip, and conditional financing may signal funder uncertainty to potential partners, potentially weakening coalition-building and institutional engagement efforts during the critical early months.

name: Stakeholder Appetite Mapping and Asymmetric Coalition Strategy
consequences: Identifying which stakeholder groups (civil society, academia, contingency planners, EU regulators, sympathetic MPs) have existing incentives to demand platform-neutral fallback paths—and which have none—allows the project to avoid wasting resources on consensus-building with reluctant incumbents. This asymmetry means the coalition can generate sufficient political and regulatory pressure around resilience and supplier concentration without needing MitID or platform operators to endorse the work. The downstream risk is that a purely adversarial posture may trigger institutional defensiveness and accelerate adoption of even tighter proprietary coupling as a counterresponse.
options: Map decision-maker incentives across government agencies, operators, and EU bodies explicitly, then allocate coalition-building effort only to constituencies with intrinsic motivation to reduce platform dependency, accepting that MitID leadership will remain hostile and focusing advocacy instead on procurement gatekeepers and continuity planners.

Construct a multi-tier coalition where civil-society and academic partners occupy the public-facing advocacy layer, while a separate confidential working group engages sympathetic insiders within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator on resilience planning without requiring them to publicly endorse platform-neutral alternatives.

Anchor the coalition around a single high-credibility institution (a major university or public research body) that signals technical rigor and independence, then use that institution's reputation to convene other stakeholders, reducing the perception that the project is a fringe advocacy effort.
review: If MitID leadership perceives the coalition as a threat to their institutional legitimacy rather than a resilience partner, they may accelerate proprietary integration to foreclose future alternatives, narrowing rather than expanding the design space.

name: Fallback Authentication Pathway Definition and Regulatory Framing
consequences: Rather than attacking platform dependency in abstract terms, the project can frame a concrete fallback path (browser-based authentication, hardware-token workflows, or platform-agnostic federation) as an essential continuity requirement under eIDAS2 and NSIS certification, shifting the conversation from sovereignty to regulatory compliance. This grounds the technical work in legal obligation rather than ideology and makes exclusion of fallback mechanisms harder to justify during procurement. The risk is that regulators may defer to operator recommendations, treating fallback as a nice-to-have rather than a compliance requirement, unless the project produces both the regulatory language and the technical proof simultaneously.
options: Collaborate with the NSIS certification body to draft or clarify interpretation of 'Substantial' level assurance requirements in ways that explicitly mandate platform-neutral or certified fallback access, making fallback a precondition for future AltID certification rather than an optional feature.

Position the fallback path as a disaster-recovery and business-continuity control required under EU digital resilience directives, appealing to risk officers and procurement auditors rather than identity architects, and embed fallback in supplier-selection criteria rather than system design.

Develop a layered authentication model where platform-mediated access remains the primary path but is supplemented by a standalone certified fallback that satisfies eIDAS2 assurance levels independently, allowing operators to claim innovation while also allowing the state to meet resilience obligations.
review: Regulators may endorse fallback in principle while allowing operators to implement it as an ineffective afterthought, meeting the letter of the requirement without the spirit of actual platform-neutral continuity.

name: Demonstrator Scope and Technical Credibility Calibration
consequences: The project's credibility depends on producing working, standards-compliant demonstrators that prove platform-neutral authentication is feasible without attempting to compete with MitID's full feature set or production maturity. Overscoping the demonstrator into a feature-rich prototype risks mission creep, budget overrun, and claims that the work is unfairly simplified compared to production systems. Underscoping it signals lack of technical substance and invites dismissal as theoretical. The balance point is narrow: demonstrators must be sufficient to defeat claims of infeasibility while remaining explicitly non-production. The risk is that stakeholders will either ignore a 'toy' system or demand it be scaled into a real replacement, collapsing the project's actual objective of establishing precedent and procurement requirements.
options: Scope each demonstrator to a single authentication workflow (e.g., one-factor browser-based login against a simulated Danish public-sector identity provider, or FIDO2 hardware-token authentication to a test environment) using off-the-shelf standards (FIDO2, OpenID Connect, SAML) and published reference implementations, explicitly documenting what is excluded (multi-factor orchestration, fraud detection, app-store distribution integration, etc.) to forestall claims of unfair simplification.

Commission an independent security audit of each demonstrator (budget 200,000–400,000 DKK per audit) before public release, with the audit explicitly covering compliance with NSIS 'Substantial' level assurance models, creating third-party technical credibility that internal claims cannot match.

Integrate the demonstrators into a physical lab environment on the project's institutional campus, with controlled access and documented chain of custody, allowing stakeholders and regulators to observe and test the systems directly rather than reviewing them only in reports, converting skepticism into witnessed evidence.
review: Even with independent security audit, stakeholders may argue that non-production demonstrators do not address operational challenges (fraud monitoring, incident response, user-support burden) that only production experience can reveal.

name: EU Alignment and Standards-Body Insertion
consequences: Denmark cannot unilaterally mandate platform-neutral identity design, but the European Digital Identity Wallet framework and eIDAS2 regulatory process offer leverage points. If the project can influence EDIWG technical working groups or EU-level standards discussions to endorse platform-neutral or fallback-capable architecture, it signals to Danish operators and regulators that supplier independence is an EU-wide expectation, not a Danish outlier position. This reduces the political isolation of the advocacy effort and creates external pressure that Danish decision-makers cannot dismiss as parochial. The downstream implication is that EU-level coordination takes time (18+ months to influence meaningful language in standards or regulatory guidance), may be diluted by other member states' priorities, and does not guarantee Danish adoption even if EU consensus exists.
options: Engage with the European Payments Council, GSM Alliance, or other relevant technical standards bodies to propose platform-neutral authentication models for public-sector identity wallets, framing the contribution as interoperability and reduced vendor lock-in benefits rather than anti-competitive arguments.

Coordinate with civil-society organizations and academic researchers in other EU member states (Germany, Estonia, France) that share digital-sovereignty concerns, collectively submitting input to the European Commission's eIDAS2 consultation processes and EDIWG working groups during formal comment periods.

Pursue formal standing as a technical contributor or observer to the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working group, positioning the project's demonstrators and feasibility work as input to EU-level architecture guidance, creating institutional visibility that elevates the Danish work beyond isolated national advocacy.
review: EU-level influence operates on a longer timeline than the project's 24-month horizon and may produce non-binding guidance that Danish operators can acknowledge without implementing.

name: Procurement Language and Contractual Lock-In Prevention
consequences: AltID procurement documents will set technical requirements and selection criteria that determine whether platform-neutral fallback access is included or excluded from the next generation of Danish identity infrastructure. If the project can contribute language to procurement RFPs, evaluation rubrics, or supplier-selection criteria that makes platform dependency a disqualifying factor or a scored disadvantage, it shifts the cost-benefit calculus for operators and vendors designing AltID solutions. This is institutional leverage without requiring technical displacement. The risk is that procurement processes in Denmark are often controlled by incumbent operators or their preferred integrators, who will actively resist neutrality requirements that complicate their supply chains or reduce their architectural control.
options: Draft a procurement-language template that defines 'platform-independent fallback authentication' with specific technical criteria (no dependence on Apple or Google APIs, compatibility with eIDAS 'Substantial' assurance without proprietary signals, documented interoperability path), then lobby to have this language embedded in the AltID RFP evaluation criteria before the formal procurement launch.

Propose a staged-procurement model where the initial AltID contract includes platform-neutral fallback as an optional enhancement with fixed pricing, shifting the decision from architecture mandate to line-item selection, making it harder for operators to claim fallback is infeasible.

Advocate for a procurement clause requiring suppliers to demonstrate fallback authentication capability via third-party testing or reference deployment before contract award, imposing upfront technical validation costs that filter out operators unwilling to support platform neutrality.
review: Procurement language alone does not guarantee compliance; operators may include fallback mechanisms that are technically compliant but operationally impractical or deliberately cumbersome to discourage use.

name: Incumbent Operator Buy-In and Institutional Reframing
consequences: Direct opposition from MitID leadership and existing identity operators is a near-certainty; the project cannot succeed by ignoring or purely attacking incumbents. Instead, reframing platform-neutral fallback as a managed-risk control and business-continuity asset that benefits operators (by reducing their single-supplier exposure and demonstrating due diligence to regulators) may reduce institutional resistance and create space for quiet cooperation on demonstrators or pilot implementations. This reframing shifts the pitch from 'your architecture is dangerous' to 'platform diversity is good risk management.' The downstream implication is that operators may agree in principle but then delay, under-resource, or sabotage implementation, treating fallback as a compliance checkbox rather than a functional system.
options: Approach MitID leadership and relevant government stakeholders privately with a proposal framing fallback authentication as a Digitaliseringsstyrelsen-mandated resilience control and disaster-recovery requirement, positioning the project's work as supporting their compliance rather than displacing their system.

Offer to conduct a confidential operational risk analysis for MitID, modeling scenarios where platform dependency creates continuity-of-service exposure (iOS policy change, Google App Store suspension in specific regions, etc.), and use this analysis to make the business case for diversification to incumbent stakeholders.

Propose a phased integration pathway where the project's fallback demonstrators are initially deployed in low-risk, non-critical public-sector authentication scenarios (e.g., citizen access to non-sensitive government portals), allowing operators and regulators to observe fallback reliability and adoption in a limited scope before scaling.
review: Incumbent operators may accept the resilience framing publicly while actively protecting their proprietary architecture behind claims that platform-neutral fallback cannot achieve the same fraud-detection and assurance standards.

name: Financing Transparency and Risk-Sharing Mechanism Design
consequences: The project is structured with gated funding (3.0 million phase one, 4.0 million phase two conditional on phase-one deliverables, 3.5 million phase three conditional on phase-two institutional engagement), which aligns funding releases with measurable progress and reduces the risk of resource waste if institutional traction does not materialize. However, this gate structure also creates a contingency risk: if phase two does not produce sufficiently credible demonstrators or if stakeholder engagement stalls, phase three funding may be withheld, leaving the project unable to influence AltID procurement decisions when they actually occur. The alternative is to pre-allocate phase three funds to resilience against political or institutional setbacks. The tension is between flexibility (keep funding gated to force disciplined progress) and resilience (secure phase three funding upfront to guarantee the advocacy layer survives technical or institutional delays).
options: Secure all 10.5 million DKK upfront from a single funder (likely Danish government digital-strategy budget or EU digital-resilience fund) with clear gating conditioned on phase-one report publication and institutional engagement, but with explicit language allowing phase-three scope to shift toward EU standards input or publication if Danish AltID traction is weak.

Diversify financing across three separate funding streams (Danish government, EU research fund, private foundation or corporate sponsor) aligned to the three phases, reducing dependency on a single decision-maker's continued commitment and buffering against mid-project political shifts in digital-policy priority.

Structure a risk-sharing arrangement where phase-two and phase-three funding are released in parallel (not strictly sequential) with declining funding levels if institutional engagement milestones are missed, ensuring sufficient resources to reach the AltID procurement window while preserving accountability for progress against political viability gates.
review: Even with diversified financing and upfront allocation, phase-three procurement intervention cannot succeed if the project has failed to establish technical credibility and coalition cohesion by month 16, meaning no financing structure can de-risk institutional inertia or incumbent operator capture.

name: Coalition Legitimacy and Anchor Institutions
consequences: A coalition anchored by credible national institutions (university, independent research body, sympathetic Folketinget members) lends authority to the project's framing and reduces the political cost to authorities of engaging with platform-neutral alternatives. Conversely, if the coalition appears too activist or ideologically driven, institutional gatekeepers (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, MitID operator) will dismiss the project as advocacy rather than policy-relevant research.
options: Partner with a major Danish university's cybersecurity or digital governance research group as the primary institutional home, ensuring access to peer-review networks and government listening posts.

Recruit a cross-party Folketinget working group on digital sovereignty to co-author or formally respond to the feasibility report, creating political cover for authorities to consider platform-neutral requirements.

Engage a respected technical standards organization (e.g., Danish Standards or EU-level body liaison) as a formal advisor to the coalition, positioning the project as standards-alignment work rather than disruption.
review: Institutional anchor status signals legitimacy but does not guarantee Digitaliseringsstyrelsen will resource AltID procurement language changes if doing so conflicts with existing vendor relationships or timeline pressures.

name: Demonstrator Realism and Scope Discipline
consequences: A lean, clearly non-production demonstrator (simulated identity provider, FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS) signals technical feasibility without threatening MitID's certification model or forcing platform vendors into defensive responses. Over-scoping into feature parity or production-like integration risks both budget bleed and accusations of attempting to undermine MitID.
options: Build a minimal mobile demonstrator that authenticates against a simulated Danish public-sector IdP using OpenID Connect and FIDO2, accompanied by explicit documentation of what it does not attempt (no MitID integration, no production certification, no app-store distribution).

Develop a browser-based fallback authenticator using hardware tokens and WebAuthn, deliberately avoiding mobile OS dependency to show that authentication security does not require app-store distribution.

Create a reference architecture document paired with one lightweight proof-of-concept (Python or similar) that illustrates the trust-model differences between platform-mediated and standards-based approaches, prioritizing conceptual clarity over engineering completeness.
review: Even a well-scoped demonstrator cannot prove production readiness or address real-world integration costs (regulatory approval, backend compatibility, operational support), so it remains a credibility signal rather than a deployment path.

name: Procurement Language Specificity and Contractual Binding
consequences: Detailed, standards-neutral procurement language (e.g., 'digital identity systems shall support authentication pathways not exclusive to any single platform distribution channel') makes it difficult for AltID procurement teams to dismiss platform-neutral requirements as vague or unspecified. Specific language also constrains future vendor responses, because refusing platform neutrality becomes a contractual compliance issue rather than a design philosophy. However, overly rigid language can trigger vendor cost claims or schedule delays.
options: Propose concrete procurement clauses referencing eIDAS2 interoperability requirements and stating that 'critical authentication pathways shall support fallback mechanisms independent of proprietary mobile OS integrity APIs', then track whether AltID's formal request-for-proposal incorporates or explicitly rejects these clauses.

Draft a supplier-neutral technical appendix to AltID procurement that defines 'platform-neutral authentication' operationally (e.g., 'capable of operation on open-source Android forks or browser-based interfaces') and require vendors to map their architecture against these criteria.

Collaborate with Danish procurement authorities to embed digital-sovereignty and resilience-based evaluation criteria in AltID vendor scoring, so that platform concentration risk becomes a measurable vendor differentiator alongside cost and timeline.
review: Contractual language can impose requirements but cannot guarantee vendors will deliver cost-competitive solutions meeting those requirements, especially if platform vendors view neutrality as a strategic threat to their ecosystem monetization.

name: External Security Review and Authority Delegation
consequences: Commissioning an independent, internationally credible security review of the demonstrators and the fallback authentication concept increases institutional trust in the project's technical claims and reduces MitID operator fears that platform-neutral alternatives are inadequately vetted. Conversely, if the external review identifies material gaps, the project loses credibility; if the review is perceived as captured or insufficiently rigorous, it becomes a liability.
options: Engage a recognized European security assessment body (e.g., ENISA-accredited firm or academic consortium) to conduct a formal security and resilience analysis of both demonstrators, with the report published openly and citing specific Danish regulatory standards (eIDAS, NSIS).

Commission a limited adversarial test of the demonstrators by a sympathetic red team from academic or non-profit security research, designed to surface realistic attack vectors and platform-switching scenarios, with findings published and addressed in phase-three revisions.

Solicit formal technical commentary from existing Danish financial-sector security officers and healthcare IT governance bodies, positioning their endorsement of fallback-authentication concepts as institutional validation rather than external review, and making their concerns part of the record.
review: External validation can enhance credibility but requires careful scoping to avoid scope creep or results that contradict the project's core claims, either of which would undermine rather than strengthen institutional leverage.

name: EU Standards Alignment and Multilateral Pressure
consequences: Positioning the project's resilience and platform-neutrality framing as aligned with European Digital Identity Wallet design principles and broader EU supply-chain resilience mandates shifts the conversation from Danish parochialism to EU-level strategic interest. This creates pressure on Danish authorities to view platform neutrality as a best practice rather than a local grievance. However, if EU-level standards bodies move slower than the AltID procurement timeline, or if they resolve against platform-neutral requirements, this strategy backfires by making Danish authorities wait for external guidance.
options: Engage the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups and identify provisions in the planned architecture or regulations that require or recommend platform-neutral access or fallback mechanisms, then amplify those provisions in Danish procurement language as EU compliance obligations.

Present the feasibility report and demonstrators to ENISA, the EU Cybersecurity Competence Centre, or relevant standards bodies as a case study in supplier-concentration resilience, seeking official commentary that validates the technical approach and strengthens Danish political cover.

Coordinate with sympathetic EU member states (e.g., countries with stronger digital-sovereignty mandates) to propose joint EU procurement language on platform neutrality in digital identity systems, creating multilateral diplomatic momentum that influences Danish decisions.
review: EU-level alignment creates external legitimacy but is slow-moving and depends on EU bodies prioritizing digital sovereignty and resilience over vendor relationships or rapid rollout timelines, neither of which is guaranteed.

name: Incumbent Operator Engagement and Reframing as Resilience
consequences: Directly engaging the MitID operator to reframe platform-neutral alternatives not as threats but as continuity insurance and risk mitigation (geopolitical platform policy changes, app-store distribution disputes, iOS/Android integrity API deprecations) can reduce defensive posturing. Successful reframing converts the operator from opponent to risk-acknowledging stakeholder. However, if the operator perceives platform neutrality as a path to customer migration or competitive substitution, reframing will fail and engagement will harden opposition.
options: Propose a joint resilience and contingency-planning working group with the MitID operator focused on 'assured access continuity if platform policies or distribution channels change', explicitly excluding any replacement of MitID for primary authentication, and presenting fallback mechanisms as MitID's own continuity safeguard.

Conduct a formal risk interview with the MitID operator documenting their existing platform-dependency concerns, geopolitical exposure scenarios, and contingency plans, then publish a sanitized version of the findings that validates the operator's own articulated risks and positions the project as solving the operator's stated problem.

Offer to include the MitID operator as a formal advisor or reviewer of the demonstrators and fallback concepts, giving the operator visibility and voice in the technical work, reducing the sense that the project is operating unilaterally behind their back.
review: Operator engagement and goodwill messaging may soften rhetoric but are unlikely to change the operator's or platform vendors' structural interest in maintaining the current high-dependency architecture, particularly if fallback mechanisms could be invoked at scale.

name: Financing Transparency and Phase-Gate Discipline
consequences: Strict adherence to phase-gating logic (phase-two funding requires phase-one deliverables and documented institutional engagement; phase-three funding requires clear AltID traction or explicit de-scoping toward publication and standards work) prevents budget drift, signals disciplined execution to institutional partners, and creates credible decision points for stakeholders to assess the project's real-world viability. Conversely, loose gating or sliding timelines will undermine funder and stakeholder confidence, especially if early phases do not produce institutional responses or procurement wins.
options: Publish a detailed phase-gate checklist by month 3 specifying exact deliverable criteria for phase-two release (feasibility report published, named institutional stakeholder engagement documented, financing plan approved), with monthly status reports against these criteria visible to funders and coalition members.

Establish a formal decision-review at month 16 with documented authority from funders and the coalition to explicitly de-scope phase three away from AltID procurement work and toward EU standards and publication if Digitaliseringsstyrelsen engagement remains non-committal, preventing the project from drifting into wishful-thinking mode.

Create a contingency-financing reserve (e.g., 10% of phase-two budget) explicitly designated for scenarios in which AltID procurement timelines slip or political priorities shift, allowing the project to extend core technical and policy work without waiting for supplementary funding requests.
review: Disciplined phase-gating prevents budget waste and signals rigor but does not resolve the underlying institutional inertia problem: even with clear gates and transparent financing, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen may continue to deprioritize platform-neutrality requirements if they conflict with vendor timelines or existing commitments.
